'''Georges Jean Franz Köhler''' ({{IPA|de|ˈʒɔʁʃ ˈkøːlɐ|-|De-Georges Köhler.ogg}}; 17 April 1946 – 1 March 1995) was a German [[biologist]] and [[immunologist]] who shared the 1984 [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] with [[César Milstein]] and [[Niels Kaj Jerne]] "for theories concerning the specificity in development and control of the immune system and the discovery of the principle for production of [[monoclonal antibody|monoclonal antibodies]]".<ref name="NobelSummary1984">{{cite web
 | title = The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1984
 | website = NobelPrize.org
 | publisher = Nobel Prize Outreach AB
 | url = https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/summary/
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref> Köhler and Milstein developed the [[hybridoma technology|hybridoma technique]], a method for producing monoclonal antibodies of predefined specificity by fusing antibody-producing [[B cell]]s with immortal [[myeloma]] cells.<ref name="KohlerMilstein1975">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Köhler
 | first1 = G.
 | last2 = Milstein
 | first2 = C.
 | title = Continuous cultures of fused cells secreting antibody of predefined specificity
 | journal = Nature
 | volume = 256
 | issue = 5517
 | pages = 495–497
 | date = 1975
 | doi = 10.1038/256495a0
 | pmid = 1172191
 | bibcode = 1975Natur.256..495K
 | s2cid = 4161444
}}</ref><ref name="NobelFacts">{{cite web
 | title = Georges J.F. Köhler – Facts
 | website = NobelPrize.org
 | publisher = Nobel Prize Outreach AB
 | url = https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/kohler/facts/
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref>

The technique became a foundational tool in [[immunology]], [[cell biology]], [[biotechnology]], medical diagnostics and antibody-based therapeutics.<ref name="Alkan2019">{{cite journal
 | last = Alkan
 | first = Sefik S.
 | title = Legends of allergy/immunology: Georges Köhler and the discovery of monoclonal antibodies
 | journal = Allergy
 | volume = 74
 | issue = 7
 | pages = 1412–1414
 | date = July 2019
 | doi = 10.1111/all.13798
 | issn = 1398-9995
 | pmid = 30920663
 | s2cid = 219281951
}}</ref><ref name="AAI">{{cite web
 | title = Georges JF Köhler, Ph.D.
 | website = American Association of Immunologists
 | url = https://www.aai.org/About/History/Notable-Members/Nobel-Laureates/GeorgesJFKohler
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref> Köhler later worked at the [[Basel Institute for Immunology]] and became director of the [[Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics|Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology]] in [[Freiburg im Breisgau]], where he remained until his death in 1995.<ref name="NobelBio">{{cite web
 | title = Georges J.F. Köhler – Biographical
 | website = NobelPrize.org
 | publisher = Nobel Prize Outreach AB
 | url = https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/kohler/biographical/
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref><ref name="MPG2016">{{cite web
 | title = Portrayal of Nobel Prize laureate and former Max Planck Director Georges Köhler
 | website = Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics
 | publisher = Max Planck Society
 | date = 6 October 2016
 | url = https://www.ie-freiburg.mpg.de/4747666/2016_10_06_koehler
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Köhler was born in [[Munich]], [[Allied-occupied Germany]], on 17 April 1946.<ref name="NobelBio" /> His father, Karl Köhler, was German, while his mother, Raymonde, came from a French family.<ref name="WhatisBioSummary">{{cite web
 | title = Professor Georges Kohler – Biographical summary
 | website = WhatisBiotechnology.org
 | url = https://www.whatisbiotechnology.org/index.php/people/summary/Kohler
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref> He studied biology at the [[University of Freiburg]], where he worked under [[Fritz Melchers]].<ref name="NobelBio" /> His doctoral research concerned the immune response and antibody production, interests that led to his later work on the generation of antibody diversity.<ref name="NobelBio" /><ref name="Melchers1995">{{cite journal
 | last = Melchers
 | first = Fritz
 | title = Georges Köhler (1946–95)
 | journal = Nature
 | volume = 374
 | issue = 6522
 | page = 498
 | date = 6 April 1995
 | doi = 10.1038/374498a0
 | pmid = 7700372
 | bibcode = 1995Natur.374..498M
}}</ref>

== Work with César Milstein ==

From April 1974 to March 1976 Köhler carried out postdoctoral research at the [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology]] in [[Cambridge]], working in the laboratory of [[César Milstein]].<ref name="NobelBio" /> His fellowship was supported by the [[European Molecular Biology Organization|EMBO]].<ref name="NobelBio" /> Milstein's laboratory was investigating the mechanisms underlying [[antibody diversity]], including how immune cells generate antibodies with different specificities.<ref name="NobelBio" /><ref name="LMB1984">{{cite web
 | title = 1984: César Milstein & Georges Köhler
 | website = MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
 | url = https://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/achievements/awards-and-prizes/nobel-prizes/1984-cesar-milstein-georges-kohler/
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref>

Köhler and Milstein sought a way to obtain continuous cultures of cells that secreted antibodies of a single defined specificity. Their solution was to fuse antibody-producing [[lymphocyte]]s from immunized animals with immortal [[myeloma]] cells, producing hybrid cells—later known as [[hybridoma]]s—that combined antibody secretion with the capacity for continuous growth in culture.<ref name="KohlerMilstein1975" /><ref name="NobelFacts" /> In 1975 they published "Continuous cultures of fused cells secreting antibody of predefined specificity" in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref name="KohlerMilstein1975" />

The hybridoma method provided a reproducible way to generate monoclonal antibodies, in contrast to conventional [[antiserum|antisera]], which contain mixtures of antibodies produced by many different immune-cell clones.<ref name="Alkan2019" /> Monoclonal antibodies could be made with uniform specificity, allowing researchers to identify, purify and measure particular molecules with high precision.<ref name="NobelFacts" /><ref name="AAI" />

== Basel Institute for Immunology ==

In April 1976 Köhler returned to Switzerland as a member of the [[Basel Institute for Immunology]], where he continued molecular and cellular work on lymphocyte hybrids.<ref name="NobelBio" /> The institute, directed by [[Niels Kaj Jerne]], was a major center for theoretical and experimental immunology.<ref name="NobelBio" /> Köhler remained at Basel for approximately a decade, continuing to investigate antibody diversity and the behavior of lymphocyte hybrid cells.<ref name="NobelBio" /><ref name="WhatisBioStory">{{cite web
 | title = The Story of César Milstein and Monoclonal Antibodies
 | website = WhatisBiotechnology.org
 | url = https://www.whatisbiotechnology.org/index.php/science/summary/milstein
 | access-date = 3 June 2026
}}</ref>

During the early 1980s he also became interested in the use of [[transgenic mouse|transgenic mice]] to study immunological mechanisms, including [[immune tolerance|self-tolerance]].<ref name="WhatisBioStory" /><ref name="Melchers1995" />

== Nobel Prize ==

Köhler, Milstein and Jerne received the 1984 [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]].<ref name="NobelSummary1984" /> Jerne was recognized for theoretical work on the specificity, development and regulation of the immune system, while Köhler and Milstein were recognized for the discovery of the principle for producing monoclonal antibodies.<ref name="NobelSummary1984" />

In his Nobel lecture, Köhler discussed the derivation and diversification of monoclonal antibodies and the scientific implications of the hybridoma technique.<ref name="KohlerNobelLecture">{{cite journal
 | last = Köhler
 | first = G.
 | title = The Nobel Lectures in Immunology. The Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine, 1984. Derivation and diversification of monoclonal antibodies
 | journal = Scandinavian Journal of Immunology
 | volume = 36
 | issue = 6
 | pages = 811–829
 | date = December 1992
 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-3083.1992.tb03140.x
 | pmid = 8434224
}}</ref> The discovery was also recognized by other awards, including the [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]], which Köhler and Milstein received in 1984.<ref name="AAI" />

== Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology ==

In 1984 Köhler became director of the [[Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics|Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology]] in [[Freiburg im Breisgau]].<ref name="MPG2016" /><ref name="NobelBio" /> He also held an association with the [[University of Freiburg]].<ref name="MPG2016" /> At Freiburg he continued work in immunology, including studies of antibody formation, lymphocyte biology and experimental models for immune regulation.<ref name="Melchers1995" />

Köhler remained director of the institute until his death.<ref name="MPG2016" />

== Personal life ==

Köhler married Claudia Reintjes in 1968.<ref name="WhatisBioSummary" /> They had three children: Katharina, Lucia and Fabian.<ref name="WhatisBioSummary" /> Biographical accounts describe him as devoted to his family as well as to scientific work; during his studies he reportedly worked as a taxi driver to support his family.<ref name="WhatisBioSummary" />

== Death ==

Köhler died in [[Freiburg im Breisgau]] on 1 March 1995 at the age of 48.<ref name="NobelBio" /><ref name="Melchers1995" /> Contemporary accounts attributed his death to a heart condition.<ref name="EichmannDeath">{{cite book
 | last = Eichmann
 | first = Klaus
 | title = Köhler's Invention
 | publisher = Birkhäuser
 | location = Basel
 | date = 2005
 | pages = 169–172
 | chapter = Köhler's death
 | isbn = 978-3-7643-7173-9
 | doi = 10.1007/3-7643-7413-6_15
}}</ref>

== Legacy ==

Köhler's collaboration with Milstein transformed experimental immunology by making it possible to produce antibodies of defined and reproducible specificity.<ref name="KohlerMilstein1975" /><ref name="Alkan2019" /> Monoclonal antibodies became essential reagents in biomedical research and clinical diagnostics and later became a major class of therapeutic agents.<ref name="NobelFacts" /><ref name="AAI" />

The hybridoma technique also helped shift immunology toward cell-based and molecular approaches, linking antibody specificity to individual lymphocyte clones and making antibodies practical tools for identifying biological molecules.<ref name="KohlerNobelLecture" /><ref name="Alkan2019" /> The [[Max Planck Society]] has described Köhler as a pioneering immunologist whose work on monoclonal antibodies had enduring consequences for science and medicine.<ref name="MPG2016" />

== Selected publications ==

* Köhler, G.; Milstein, C. "Continuous cultures of fused cells secreting antibody of predefined specificity." ''Nature''. 1975.<ref name="KohlerMilstein1975" />
* Köhler, G. "The Nobel Lectures in Immunology. The Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine, 1984. Derivation and diversification of monoclonal antibodies." ''Scandinavian Journal of Immunology''. 1992.<ref name="KohlerNobelLecture" />
